events.text: John Napier publishes his first description of logarithms
Fibonacci's Liber Abaci brings Hindu-Arabic numerals to European readers
Andrew Wiles announces his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem at Cambridge
Newton's Principia sets out his laws of motion and universal gravitation

reveal.explanation: Fibonacci carried Hindu-Arabic numerals into Europe in 1202, and Napier set out his logarithms four centuries later in 1614. Newton's Principia followed in 1687, while Wiles waited until 1993 to tell a Cambridge lecture room that Fermat's Last Theorem had been proved.

sources.excerpt: The Liber Abaci or Liber Abbaci (Latin for "The Book of Calculation") was a 1202 Latin work on arithmetic by Leonardo of Pisa, posthumously known as Fibonacci.
The method of logarithms was publicly propounded by John Napier in 1614, in a book titled Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (Description of the Wonderful Canon of Logarithms).
The Principia is written in Latin and comprises three volumes, and was authorized (imprimatur) by Samuel Pepys, then-president of the Royal Society on 5 July 1686 and first published in 1687.

During 21–23 June 1993, Wiles announced and presented his proof of the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture for semistable elliptic curves, and hence of Fermat's Last Theorem, over the course of three lectures delivered at the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences in Cambridge, England.
